question: Autoclave uses:
explanation:
• An autoclave sterilises with saturated steam under pressure, typically 121°C at 15 psi for 15 minutes, because moist heat coagulates microbial proteins much faster than dry heat.
• Dry heat at 160°C is the hot air oven, a separate method, and UV light only surface-disinfects.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e — Sterilisation and Disinfection

question: Hot air oven is used for:
explanation:
• A hot air oven (160°C for 2 hours) is used for items that steam cannot penetrate or would spoil — glassware, metal instruments, oils, powders and greases.
• Rubber gloves, catheters and endoscopes are heat-labile and need autoclaving or low-temperature chemical methods instead.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e — Sterilisation and Disinfection

question: Gram-negative bacteria have:
options: A. Thick peptidoglycan, no outer membrane
B. Thin peptidoglycan and outer membrane with LPS
explanation:
• Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer plus an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin), so the crystal violet–iodine complex is washed out by the decolouriser and they take the pink counterstain.
• Gram-positive organisms have thick peptidoglycan and no outer membrane, and acid-fast bacilli have a waxy mycolic acid wall.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e — Morphology and Physiology of Bacteria: The Bacterial Cell Wall

question: Hepatitis B transmission includes:
explanation:
• Hepatitis B is blood-borne, spreading through infected blood and body fluids — needlestick injury and unsafe injections, transfusion, sexual contact and perinatal transmission from mother to baby.
• Hepatitis A and E are the faeco-orally transmitted hepatitis viruses.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e — Hepatitis Viruses

question: Mantoux test measures:
options: B. Delayed hypersensitivity to TB antigens
explanation:
• The Mantoux test injects 5 TU of PPD intradermally and is read at 48–72 hours by measuring induration, so it detects type IV delayed (cell-mediated) hypersensitivity to tubercular antigens.
• A positive result indicates infection or prior BCG, not active disease, and it does not measure antibody.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e — Mycobacterium tuberculosis: Tuberculin Testing

question: CD4 cells are primarily:
explanation:
• CD4 is the surface marker of helper T lymphocytes, the principal cell infected and destroyed by HIV, which is why the CD4 count is used to stage disease and monitor therapy.
• Cytotoxic T cells carry CD8 instead.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e — Human Immunodeficiency Virus

question: Malaria vector:
explanation:
• Malaria is transmitted by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito, which characteristically bites at night.
• Culex transmits filariasis and Japanese encephalitis, while Aedes transmits dengue, chikungunya and Zika.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e — Malaria Parasites (Plasmodium)

question: Passive immunity example:
explanation:
• Passive immunity means ready-made antibody is transferred to the host rather than produced by it, as with maternal IgG crossing the placenta, immunoglobulin or antiserum.
• It acts immediately but is short-lived, whereas vaccines and natural infection produce active immunity with immunological memory.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e — Immunity to Infection: Active and Passive Immunity

question: ELISA is used to detect:
options: B. Antigens or antibodies in serum
explanation:
• ELISA uses an enzyme-labelled antibody or antigen with a colour-producing substrate to detect and quantify either antigen or antibody in serum, and is the standard screening test for HIV, hepatitis B and dengue.
• Culture and microscopy, not ELISA, are used to demonstrate organisms directly.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e — Antigen-Antibody Reactions: Immunoassays

question: Spores are best destroyed by:
explanation:
• Bacterial spores survive boiling for a few minutes, alcohol rubs and soap washing, so only sporicidal methods such as autoclaving at 121°C, dry heat, glutaraldehyde or ethylene oxide reliably destroy them.
• This is why alcohol hand rub is ineffective against Clostridioides difficile and hand washing with soap and water is required instead.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e — Sterilisation and Disinfection

question: Microbiology Q11: Which is a gram-positive coccus in clusters?
explanation:
• Staph aureus: gram-positive cocci in clusters.
• Strep: chains.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e — Staphylococcus

question: As per the Bio-Medical Waste (Management) Rules, 2016, a used hypodermic needle must be discarded into a:
explanation: Waste sharps, including needles, scalpel blades and any contaminated sharp metal, belong to the white category and must go into a translucent, puncture-proof, leak-proof container. The red bag is the tempting alternative because the rest of the syringe goes there, but red is only for contaminated recyclable plastic such as the syringe barrel, tubing and catheters, and putting a needle in a plastic bag exposes waste handlers to needle-stick injury.
citation: MoHFW Bio-Medical Waste (Management) Rules 2016 - Schedule I

question: The biological indicator used to confirm that an autoclave cycle has been effective is spores of:
explanation: Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores are the most heat-resistant test organism for moist heat, and their failure to grow after processing proves the load reached sterilising conditions. Bacillus atrophaeus is the usual wrong answer because it is also a spore-forming indicator, but it is used to validate dry heat in the hot air oven and ethylene oxide sterilisation, not steam under pressure.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e - Sterilisation and Disinfection

question: A flexible fibreoptic endoscope cannot be autoclaved. The agent of choice for its high-level disinfection is:
explanation: Two per cent alkaline glutaraldehyde achieves high-level disinfection in about twenty minutes, kills vegetative bacteria, fungi and viruses, and does not corrode lenses or damage rubber and plastic parts. Sodium hypochlorite is the tempting choice since it is a good general disinfectant, but it corrodes the metal parts of instruments and is rapidly inactivated by organic matter, so it is reserved for surfaces and spills.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e - Sterilisation and Disinfection

question: A nurse's hands are visibly soiled with blood after removing an intravenous cannula. Hand hygiene should be performed with:
options: A. An alcohol-based hand rub for 20 to 30 seconds
B. Soap and water for 40 to 60 seconds
C. A dry wipe followed by fresh gloves
D. A quick rinse under running water alone
explanation: WHO specifies handwashing with soap and running water for 40 to 60 seconds whenever hands are visibly soiled, since mechanical washing is needed to remove blood and organic matter. An alcohol-based rub is the tempting answer because it is faster and is preferred at most other moments, but alcohol is inactivated by organic soil and does not remove spores such as those of Clostridioides difficile.
citation: WHO Guidelines on Hand Hygiene in Health Care

question: The single most effective measure for preventing catheter-associated urinary tract infection is:
options: A. Changing the catheter routinely every 48 hours
B. Instilling an antiseptic solution into the drainage bag
C. Giving prophylactic antibiotics while the catheter is in place
D. Removing the catheter as soon as it is no longer needed
explanation: Risk of bacteriuria rises with every additional catheter day, so limiting the duration of catheterisation prevents more infection than any other intervention. Routine scheduled catheter changes are the tempting answer, but each change breaks the closed system and introduces organisms; likewise prophylactic antibiotics merely select for resistant flora without lowering infection rates.
citation: CDC/HICPAC Guideline for Prevention of Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections

question: A patient with sputum smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis is admitted to the ward. The correct transmission-based precaution is:
options: B. Contact precautions with gown and gloves
C. Airborne precautions, with staff wearing an N95 respirator in a well-ventilated or negative-pressure room
D. Droplet precautions, with staff wearing a surgical mask
explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis spreads in droplet nuclei under five micrometres that stay suspended in room air for hours and travel on air currents, so ventilation plus a fit-tested N95 respirator is required. Droplet precautions with a surgical mask is the common wrong answer: a surgical mask does not filter droplet nuclei and protects others from the wearer, which is why the patient wears one for source control while staff wear the N95.
citation: MoHFW National Guidelines on Airborne Infection Control in Healthcare and Other Settings

question: A farmer develops trismus, neck stiffness and risus sardonicus about ten days after a deep nail-prick injury to the foot. The causative organism is:
explanation: Clostridium tetani is an anaerobic spore-forming bacillus abundant in soil, and a deep puncture wound gives it the low-oxygen conditions it needs; its toxin tetanospasmin blocks release of the inhibitory transmitters GABA and glycine, producing the sustained spasm and lockjaw described. Clostridium botulinum is the tempting relative, but its toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction and causes descending flaccid paralysis, the exact opposite picture.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e - Clostridium

question: During an outbreak, an adult presents with profuse painless watery stools resembling rice water and rapidly becomes dehydrated. The most likely organism is:
explanation: Cholera toxin permanently activates adenylate cyclase in enterocytes, driving massive secretion of isotonic fluid, so the stool is painless, voluminous and flecked with mucus, and dehydration develops within hours. Shigella is the tempting outbreak organism, but it invades the colonic mucosa and produces small-volume stools with blood, mucus, fever and tenesmus rather than painless watery purging.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e - Vibrio

question: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is defined as disease caused by an organism resistant to at least:
explanation: MDR-TB means resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampicin, the two most powerful first-line drugs, with or without resistance to others; such patients need a longer regimen with second-line agents. Resistance to all four first-line drugs is the tempting answer because it sounds like the worst case, but that is not required by the definition, and waiting for it would delay appropriate treatment.
citation: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on Tuberculosis - Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis Treatment

question: Which of the following vaccines is damaged by freezing and must never be stored in the freezer compartment?
explanation: Hepatitis B, like DPT, TT and pentavalent, is an aluminium-adsorbed vaccine; freezing breaks up the adsorbed antigen irreversibly, and the shake test is used to detect such damaged vials, which must be discarded. Oral polio vaccine is the tempting answer because it is the most heat-sensitive vaccine of all, but heat sensitivity is the opposite problem, and OPV is in fact kept in the freezer or the coldest part of the cold chain.
citation: MoHFW Universal Immunization Programme - Handbook for Vaccine and Cold Chain Handlers

question: A patient in the first week of continuous fever is suspected to have enteric fever. The investigation most likely to confirm the diagnosis at this stage is:
explanation: Bacteraemia is maximal in the first week, so blood culture is positive in the great majority of untreated cases and also yields the isolate for sensitivity testing. The Widal test is the tempting choice because it is cheap and widely ordered, but agglutinins appear only towards the end of the first week and rise later, and a single titre is unreliable in an endemic population; stool and urine cultures become useful only in the second and third weeks.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e - Salmonella

question: A midstream urine sample collected for culture cannot be transported to the laboratory within two hours. It should be:
options: A. Left at room temperature until the morning round
B. Refrigerated at 2 to 8 degrees Celsius for up to 24 hours
C. Frozen at minus 20 degrees Celsius
D. Preserved by adding a few drops of formalin
explanation: Urine is an excellent culture medium, so contaminants multiply at room temperature and produce falsely high colony counts that can be misreported as infection; refrigeration holds the bacterial count steady until the sample is plated. Formalin is the tempting preservative, but it is a fixative that kills the organisms and makes culture impossible, and freezing similarly destroys the pathogens being sought.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e - Collection and Transport of Specimens

question: A nurse sustains a needle-stick injury from a known HIV-positive patient. Post-exposure prophylaxis should be started:
options: A. Only after the nurse's own HIV test becomes positive
B. Within seven days of the exposure
C. As soon as possible, preferably within two hours and not beyond 72 hours
D. At the six-week follow-up visit
explanation: Prophylaxis works only before the virus establishes systemic infection, so the first dose of the 28-day antiretroviral regimen should ideally be given within two hours and is not recommended after 72 hours. Waiting for the exposed nurse to test positive is the trap: her baseline test is drawn to document pre-existing status, but by the time it turns positive infection is established and prophylaxis is useless.
citation: NACO National Technical Guidelines on Anti-Retroviral Treatment - Post-Exposure Prophylaxis

question: Three months after completing the hepatitis B vaccine course, which serological marker confirms that a health worker is protected?
explanation: The vaccine contains only surface antigen, so a successful response shows up as anti-HBs, and a titre of 10 mIU/mL or more is taken as protective. HBsAg is the tempting answer because it is the marker everyone associates with hepatitis B, but its presence signifies current infection rather than immunity; anti-HBc develops only after natural infection and is therefore absent in a vaccinated person.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e - Hepatitis Viruses

question: A patient has had fever for three days and dengue is suspected. The most appropriate confirmatory test at this stage is:
explanation: The NS1 antigen circulates from the first day of fever until about day five, making it the test of choice in the early febrile phase. IgM by MAC-ELISA is the tempting answer, but antibody becomes detectable only after about the fifth day, so ordering it on day three commonly yields a false negative and falsely reassures the team.
citation: NVBDCP National Guidelines for Clinical Management of Dengue Fever

question: A patient from an endemic area has high fever with altered sensorium, and the peripheral smear shows ring forms with several parasites within single red cells. The species responsible for cerebral malaria is:
explanation: Plasmodium falciparum invades red cells of every age, so parasite loads become very high, and infected cells develop knobs that make them adhere to capillary endothelium and sequester in cerebral vessels, producing coma. Plasmodium vivax is the tempting answer as the commonest species in much of India, but it infects only young red cells, keeps parasitaemia low and causes relapses from liver hypnozoites rather than cerebral disease.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e - Plasmodium

question: A patient on prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics develops white, curd-like patches on the tongue and buccal mucosa that leave a raw bleeding surface when scraped. The most likely causative organism is:
explanation: Broad-spectrum antibiotics suppress the normal bacterial flora and allow Candida albicans, a commensal yeast, to overgrow as oral thrush; a KOH mount or Gram stain of the scraping shows budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae. Herpes simplex is the tempting alternative for oral lesions, but it produces painful vesicles that ulcerate and cannot be wiped off as removable plaques.
citation: Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e - Medical Mycology
